newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Britain proposes anti-terrorism declaration at U.N..
newsitem.headline: Britain proposes anti-terrorism declaration at U.N..

text.p: Britain proposed a declaration in the General Assembly's legal committee on Thursday aimed at ensuring countries do not become havens for people helping organise terrorist acts against other states.

"It seeks to make clear that those who finance, plan and incite terrorist acts are acting contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations," the legal advisor of Britain's U.N. mission, Elizabeth Wilmshurst, told the committee.

"Such people, like those who are actually engaged in committing acts of terrorist violence themselves, cannot demand the protection of the Refugee Convention of 1951," she said, referring to a treaty defining the status of refugees.
The proposed declaration, if approved, would be appended to a resolution dealing with terrorism to be adopted by the committee and later endorsed by the Assembly plenary.

Britain was anxious the declaration should not be portrayed as in any way weakening the protection afforded by the refugee convention, Wilmshurst said, citing her country's long record of giving asylum to people fleeing persecution.
But it might be taken into account by courts, for example, when interpreting the refugee convention, she added.

The problem it addressed was of "individuals escaping from one state and setting up in another to plan or fund or incite terrorist acts to be carried out in their home state or elsewhere," she said, without referring to any specific cases.
Britain tried earlier this year to deport a fundamentalist Saudi Arabian dissident, Mohammad al-Masari, whose outspoken attacks on the Saudi royal family strained relations between the two countries.

The deportation move was overruled by an immigration appeals tribunal. Masari later supported what he called the intellectual arguments behind a bomb attack in June in the Saudi city of Dhahran which killed 19 American soldiers.
